title: Stress-energy, conservation laws and the covariant derivative in curvilinear coordinates
summary: Volume elements and Gauss's theorem; electrodynamics in geometric language; the stress-energy tensor, its symmetry, dust and the perfect fluid; ∂_μ T^μν = 0 and its Newtonian limit (continuity and Euler); curvilinear coordinates on the flat plane, varying basis vectors and the Christoffel symbol; the covariant derivative, metric compatibility and the Christoffel formula; the divergence in polar coordinates. Flat spacetime throughout.

objectives.description: Construct the stress-energy tensors of dust and of a perfect fluid, verify their rest-frame components, and interpret each component in a moving frame.
Derive the continuity and Euler equations from ∂_μ T^μν = 0, stating the two approximations used and what each neglects.
Compute Christoffel symbols from varying basis vectors and from the metric formula, and show the two agree in polar and spherical coordinates.
Define the covariant derivative of vectors, one-forms and tensors, prove metric compatibility implies the Christoffel formula, and derive the divergence and Laplacian in curvilinear coordinates.
Explain why Γ is not a tensor and why ∇ is, and state precisely why none of this is curvature.

preparation.description: Read the Lecture Guide's synopses of Lectures 4 and 5 (PDF page 1): volume elements and the Levi-Civita tensor, integral and differential conservation laws, electrodynamics in geometric language, the stress-energy tensor and the perfect fluid; symmetry and meaning of T's components, conservation of energy and momentum, curvilinear coordinates, the Christoffel symbol and the covariant derivative, ∇g = 0 from the equivalence principle.
Watch Lecture 4: Volumes and Volume Elements; Conservation Laws (transcript available).
Watch Lecture 5: The Stress Energy Tensor and the Christoffel Symbol (transcript available).
Second account: Tong, General Relativity, Chapter 2 Introducing Differential Geometry (reference-only), for the mathematician's view of vector fields and bases.
Optional: Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity, Chapter 1 (stress-energy in special relativity) and the opening of Chapter 3 Curvature (the covariant derivative), reference-only.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: all non-zero Christoffel symbols of flat 3-space in spherical coordinates derived, the divergence and Laplacian obtained from the covariant derivative, and both test-function checks passed.

commonMisconceptions.correction: Polar coordinates on the flat plane have Γ^r_θθ = −r and Γ^θ_rθ = 1/r. Γ records how coordinate basis vectors vary; curvature is the obstruction to making all Γ vanish in a neighbourhood, not at a point or in one coordinate system.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Γ is a tensor because it has three indices.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Its transformation law has an inhomogeneous term (it vanishes in Cartesian coordinates and not in polar ones on the same plane). The inhomogeneous term cancels that of ∂_β V^μ, so ∇_β V^μ is a tensor although neither piece is.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The pressure in T^μν only appears in the spatial diagonal, so it cannot affect energy or momentum conservation.
commonMisconceptions.correction: In (ρ + P)u^μu^ν + Pη^μν the pressure also multiplies u^μu^ν; it contributes to the inertia of a moving fluid and, later, to gravity. Only in the limit P ≪ ρc² does it drop out of the continuity equation.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Metric compatibility ∇g = 0 is an extra postulate.
commonMisconceptions.correction: On flat space it is a theorem: ∇ = ∂ in Cartesian coordinates where g is constant, and the statement is tensorial. In general relativity the Guide imposes it by appeal to the equivalence principle (local flatness), which is where the postulate enters.
